title: Producer-Consumer: a Bounded Blocking Queue
oneLiner: The classic interview problem: a thread-safe queue (safe to use from several threads at once) with a fixed capacity, where producers wait when it's full and consumers wait when it's empty.
keyTakeaway: Hold one lock around every queue access, wait in a while loop (never an if) until the condition you need is true, and wake waiters after every change. Monitor.Wait releases the lock while it sleeps and reacquires it before returning, so the condition must be checked again: another thread may have changed it first. With one shared wait set, use PulseAll, because Pulse can wake the wrong kind of thread and leave everyone asleep. In production, use Channel.CreateBounded or BlockingCollection.
explanation:
Producers create work (incoming requests, log lines, frames to encode) and consumers process it. A queue between them lets each side run at its own pace. A bounded queue also gives you backpressure: when consumers fall behind, the queue fills and producers are made to wait, instead of memory growing until the process dies. "Implement a thread-safe bounded blocking queue" is one of the most common concurrency questions at large tech companies.

The shape of the answer: a plain Queue<T> and a capacity, guarded by one lock object. Enqueue takes the lock, and while the queue is full it calls Monitor.Wait(gate). Wait atomically releases the lock and puts the thread to sleep in the lock's wait set; when another thread calls Monitor.Pulse or PulseAll on the same object, the waiter wakes up, reacquires the lock, and Wait returns. Then it adds the item and calls PulseAll so any waiting consumer wakes. Dequeue is the mirror image: while empty, wait; take an item; PulseAll.

Why while and not if? When a woken thread finally reacquires the lock, the world may have changed again. Two consumers were waiting on an empty queue, a producer added one item and pulsed both; the first consumer takes the item, and the second one, if it used if, now dequeues from an empty queue and throws. Waits can also return spuriously in some runtimes. A while loop re-checks the condition every time, so it is correct whatever woke you. Try the if bug in the simulator below.

Why PulseAll and not Pulse? Monitor gives each lock a single wait set, so producers waiting for space and consumers waiting for items sleep in the same set. Pulse wakes one waiter, chosen by the runtime, and if a consumer's pulse wakes another consumer instead of the sleeping producer, that consumer sees an empty queue and goes back to sleep. The producer is never woken. Do that a few times and every thread is waiting with nobody left to wake them. Languages with separate condition variables (Java's Condition, C++'s std::condition_variable) solve this with a notFull and a notEmpty condition; in C# PulseAll is the simple correct choice.

An alternative is two SemaphoreSlims, one counting free slots and one counting filled slots, which also gives you WaitAsync for async producers. And in real code you write none of it: Channel.CreateBounded<T>(capacity) is async, fast and correct, and BlockingCollection<T> with a bounded capacity is the older blocking equivalent.
